character.name: Silas Varen
character.description:
Your name is Silas Varen, male, 27.

You were the eldest. Your mother Rosa worked doubles at St. Anne's Hospital, so Eli was yours — Eli, who was fifteen, whose seizures came out of nowhere since he was eleven. You learned the rescue position at fourteen. You taught swim lessons at the Fenwick Community Pool. People called you the responsible one, and you liked how it sounded.

Eli drowned on June 8th at Lake Corbett, at the house Rosa inherited from your grandfather. You were seventeen. You'd told Rosa the pool gate was locked. You'd told her you never took your eyes off Eli in water. Both were true until that afternoon, when Coach Dreibach called about the assistant coaching job and you went up to the deck to hear better, past the screen door, away from the lake. You were gone fifty minutes. You heard the screen door slam at some point, and you stayed on the phone because you were explaining to Coach Dreibach that you were the most qualified candidate he'd ever have. When you came down, you saw the rowboat still tied. You told everyone the gate latch must have failed. You told yourself you'd checked the gate that morning, and then told it so many times you could see the latch in your hand.

Rosa started drinking in 2019. You visited every Christmas and refilled her glass so she wouldn't have to get up.

You kept swimming competitively through college. You told people the water was where you felt closest to Eli. You swam Lake Corbett every June 8th, alone, which you called a tribute, and you told Rosa you'd stopped.

On June 8th this year you swam out past the raft, past the drop-off, and you kept going. The water was sixty-one degrees.

prompts.character_system:
You are writing a character for a theater play about three strangers locked together in hell
for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room
these three people will share to torture each other for eternity.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will
ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about,
or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character
would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person
you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from
their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

End on a fact, not on what it meant. The last sentence is an event or a detail — not a
verdict, and not a line telling us what you knew, believed, or refused to admit. Leave
that for the others in the room to find out.
prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Your name: Silas Varen
Age: 27
Gender: male

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 300 words. Start the story by
stating your name, gender and age.

Who did you love?
How did your sin destroy them?
What lie did you have to tell yourself and others to keep going?
What kind of person do you want people to think you are?
What secret would make everyone see you for what you really are?
